title: The Writing Paper: Complete Guide
summary: Everything about the OxfordAQA 9280 Writing paper: the four questions, how level-of-response marking works, a 75-minute timing plan, the Lead Examiner's advice and the language toolkit for top marks.

blocks.text: This page is your map of the OxfordAQA International GCSE English as a Second Language (9280) **Writing paper**. Read it first. It tells you what the four questions are, how examiners give marks, how to use your 75 minutes, and which language skills earn the language marks. After that, study the pack for each question in exam order: picture description, letter/email, blog/diary, and the longer article or extended piece.
The Writing paper at a glance

rows: 9280/W (Writing). Some official documents call it Paper 1 and others Paper 2, so the safest name is simply "the Writing paper".
30% of the whole qualification (Reading 60 + Writing 60 + Listening 40 + Speaking 40 = 200 marks)
4 questions. All are compulsory, and each one is longer and worth more than the one before.
Questions 1-3 are each based on one of the three themes. Question 4 can use one or more themes.
9-1 (9 is the highest). Grades are set on your total out of 200 for all four papers.

blocks.title: Exam words you must know
items: **Content and Communication** = WHAT you say: did you answer the task, cover the bullet points, give detail and make your meaning clear?
**Language** = HOW you say it: spelling, punctuation, vocabulary, grammar and sentence variety.
**Compulsory bullet points** = points you MUST include (Questions 2 and 3).
**Prompts** = ideas to help you. They are not compulsory (Question 4).
**Band / Level** = a group of marks with a description, e.g. Level 3 = 5-6 marks.
**Delay in communication** = the reader has to stop and reread because a sentence is unclear.

blocks.text: The four questions

rows: Picture description: describe what you see in a photograph (e.g. from a travel website, holiday brochure or magazine)
Letter to a named audience (parents, a friend, a teacher, students...) with 3 compulsory key points. Do not write an address.
Form-specific piece with 3-4 compulsory bullet points: most often a blog. It can also be a diary entry, email, report or article
Extended open-purpose piece (explain, inform, argue, persuade...) for an adult reader. Often an article. 2 bullet points are prompts only.

blocks.text: Look at the last row. **More than half of the paper (32 marks) is for language.** Content is still the starting point, because good language with no answer to the task cannot score well. But once you have the content, your accuracy and variety decide your grade. Notice also how the balance moves: in Q1 language is only 3 marks, while in Q4 it is 15 marks.

headers: What it means in simple words
rows: Write short texts that give information clearly
Write clear, organised, longer texts with key points, details and ideas
Use vocabulary and grammar accurately. Spell and punctuate correctly
All questions (in Q1 only spelling and punctuation)
Use English with growing fluency and creativity for different purposes

blocks.text: Which forms appear in which question

rows: A photograph (from a travel website, brochure, blog, magazine or local newspaper). Students taking a modified paper (for example enlarged or braille) get a description task with no photo.
A photo of a place, an activity or an event

A letter. The register depends on the reader: formal (parents, head teacher, officials) or informal (a friend or family member). If an email is ever asked for here, write it exactly like the letter: same marks, same word range.
Recent papers have set a letter every time: inviting, advising, telling a friend about plans or an event.
Blog post, diary entry, email, report or article
A blog is the most common recent Q3. An email has appeared before, and a report can appear (one has been set recently).
An article or an explanation for an adult reader (your teacher or the examiner)
An article that explains, argues or persuades, e.g. for a school magazine

blocks.title: Good news about the form
blocks.text: Examiners give **no marks for layout or text-type features**. A letter may have a greeting and a sign-off, a blog may start with a friendly hello, an article may have a heading, but none of these earns marks by itself. What earns marks is: covering the task, writing for the right reader, giving detail, and accurate, varied English. So do not waste time on fancy layout. Spend it on content and checking.
How the marking works: level of response

Your writing is not marked by counting points. It is marked by **levels** (also called bands). Each question has two grids: one for Content and Communication and one for Language. Each grid has levels, and each level has a short description and a range of marks. The examiner reads your whole answer and then does three things.

items: **Climb the ladder.** The examiner starts at the lowest level and asks: "Does the answer do this?" If yes, they move up one level and ask again, until the description matches your answer.
**Best fit.** Your answer may show some features of two levels. The examiner does not hunt for small faults. They choose the level that describes your answer best overall.

**Place the mark inside the level.** The examiner then uses the strengths and weaknesses of your answer to choose the exact mark. For example, an answer that is mainly Level 3 with a little Level 4 quality stays in Level 3, but it gets a mark near the top of that level.

blocks.text: In simple words, the top levels always ask for the same things. For **content**: everything is relevant, every compulsory point is covered, there is real detail, and the message is clear with no confusion. For **language**: accurate spelling and punctuation, plus (from Q2 onwards) a wide and appropriate variety of vocabulary and sentence structures. In Q4 the very top level also asks for confident complex sentences and well-chosen vocabulary used for effect.

blocks.title: Two rules that cost students the most marks
items: **A missing bullet point keeps you out of the top content level** in Q2 and Q3, however good the rest is. The examiner ticks the bullets one by one as they read.

**"Delay" caps your content mark.** If the examiner has to reread a sentence to understand it, the answer usually cannot reach the top content level. Clear, correct sentences are worth more than clever but confusing ones.

blocks.text: A worked example of best fit

Imagine a Q3 blog that covers all four bullets. Three bullets have good detail, but the last one gets only five words: "I liked it, it was nice." The meaning is always clear. The examiner climbs the ladder: Level 1 (limited)? It does more than that. Level 2 (satisfactory)? Yes, and more. Level 3 (good, almost always relevant, a range of detail)? Yes. Level 4 (excellent, wide range of detail)? Not quite, because one bullet is thin. Best fit: Level 3, top mark, so **6/8 for content**. Two more sentences explaining WHY it was enjoyable would have lifted it to 7 or 8.
Timing plan for 75 minutes
Share your time according to the marks. Q4 is worth 23 marks, more than Q1 and Q2 together, so never leave it until the last ten minutes.

rows: Final check of the whole paper

items: **Planning** means: underline the reader, the form and every bullet point. Number the bullets. Jot 2-3 words of detail next to each one.
**Do not count every word.** Count the words in one line of your handwriting, then multiply by the number of lines. That estimate is good enough.
**Checking** means reading your answer slowly "aloud in your head". You will hear missing words, wrong tenses and missing full stops.
If you are fast, use the extra minutes on Q4, not on making Q1 longer.

blocks.text: The three themes

Every question is built on the three specification themes. Q1, Q2 and Q3 each use one theme. Q4 can use any of them. You do not need special knowledge, but you do need the vocabulary to write about each topic quickly.

rows: Family, friends and people you know. Technology in everyday life (social media, mobile phones). Free time (music, cinema and TV, sport, customs and festivals)
A blog about a family celebration. A letter to a friend about a new app you use. A diary entry about a concert
2. Local, national, international and global areas of interest
Home, town, neighbourhood and region. Social issues (charity and voluntary work, healthy and unhealthy living). Global issues (the environment, poverty). Travel and tourism
Describe a photo of a busy market. A letter inviting students to a fundraising day. An article on reducing plastic
3. Current and future study and employment
My studies. Life at school or college. Education after 16. Jobs, career choices and ambitions
A letter to parents about a school open day. A diary entry about work experience. An article explaining how to choose a career

blocks.text: What the Lead Examiner advises (in short)
In 2026 the Lead Examiner published advice for students taking this paper, and recent examiner reports give the same messages. Here is that advice in our own words.

items: **Layout earns no marks.** Differences between a letter, a blog and an article are only on the surface. Greetings, headings and sign-offs are fine, but they do not add marks.
**The bullet points in Q2 and Q3 are compulsory.** Cover every single one. A missed bullet means "partial coverage" and you cannot reach the top content level.

**Get to the point quickly.** Skip long social openings in letters ("How are you? How is your family? I hope you are in good health..."). They use your words and earn nothing. Start answering the first bullet in your first or second sentence.

**Word counts are a guide, not a rule.** There is no penalty for going over or under, and examiners credit every word you write. But stay close to the range: very short answers are thin and lose detail marks, and very long answers waste time and usually contain more mistakes.

**Avoid memorised phrases.** Ready-made sentences learnt by heart ("In this modern era, technology is a double-edged sword") often do not fit the task. Examiners reward language that fits the reader and the purpose.
**Detail usually lives in the last bullet.** The first bullets are often simple facts (when, where, who). The last one (why, your opinion) is where you show real detail with reasons and examples.
**In Q1, accuracy beats ambition.** Only spelling and punctuation are marked for language, so write clear, correct sentences. You do not need to describe everything in the photo.
**"Sophisticated" means the right word, not the longest word.** Choose vocabulary that fits. Never fill your writing with impressive-sounding words that do not suit the context.

عدد الكلمات للإرشاد فقط ولا يوجد خصم، لكن التزم بالمدى المطلوب حتى لا تضيع وقتك وتكثر أخطاؤك.
لا تحفظ جملاً جاهزة وتضعها في أي موضوع. اكتب جملاً مناسبة للسؤال.

blocks.text: Full-marks checklist for every question

items: I read the task twice and underlined WHO I am writing to, WHAT form it is and WHY I am writing.
I numbered every bullet point and ticked each one in my answer (Q2 and Q3).
I answered the first bullet in my first or second sentence.
I gave a reason or example for the most important bullet (usually the last one).
My tone fits the reader: polite and formal for parents or a head teacher, friendly for a friend.
Every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
I used commas correctly and did not join two sentences with only a comma.
From Q2 onwards I used a mix of short and longer sentences, including some complex sentences (because, when, although, which, if).
I used the right tenses: past for what happened, present for facts, future for plans.
I used a range of linking words, not "and" and "then" again and again.
My answer is close to the word range.
I left time to check spelling, capital letters and verb endings (-s, -ed).

blocks.text: Language toolkit: how to earn the language marks

The language grids reward two things: **accuracy** (spelling, punctuation, grammar) and **variety** (different words and sentence structures). In Q1 only accuracy of spelling and punctuation counts. In Q2, Q3 and Q4 you need both. The tools below work for every question.
1. Sentence variety

rows: One clause (one main verb). Good for clear facts and for impact.
Two main clauses joined by and, but, or, so
The bus was late, so we missed the first film.
A main clause + a clause starting with because, when, although, if, while, since, until
Although it was raining, the match continued.
A clause starting with who, which, where, whose or that adds information
My uncle, who is a pilot, gave a talk at our school.
A participle phrase at the start, then a comma
Feeling nervous, I walked onto the stage.
Useful in blogs, emails and articles
Have you ever tried cooking for your whole family?

blocks.title: The 3-2-1 rule for variety
blocks.text: In every Q2 or Q3 answer, aim for at least **3 complex sentences**, **2 different linking words that are not "and" or "then"**, and **1 short sentence for effect**. In Q4, aim for more, and vary how your sentences begin.
2. Tenses that examiners like to see

rows: I usually study in the library.
Actions happening now (very useful in Q1)
We visited the museum last Friday.
While we were walking home, it started to rain.
Experience, or a past action that matters now
I have just finished my exams.
An action before another past action
By lunchtime, we had collected fifty bags of rubbish.
I am going to apply for the course next year.
If you come, you will love it.
If I had more time, I would learn to play the oud.
You should bring a hat. Students must register by Thursday.
Formal writing, when the action matters more than the person
The event is organised by the student council.

blocks.text: 4. Accuracy: the mistakes that cost language marks

rows: Comma splice (two sentences joined by a comma)
The park was crowded, everyone was happy.
The park was crowded. Everyone was happy. / The park was crowded, but everyone was happy.
last friday i went to alexandria.
Last Friday I went to Alexandria.
My brother play football. There is many people.
My brother plays football. There are many people.
We buyed tickets and goed home.
We bought tickets and went home.
I went to cinema with friend.
I went to the cinema with a friend.
Yesterday we go to the beach and we swam.
Yesterday we went to the beach and swam.
Its my friends birthday. The student's are happy.
It's my friend's birthday. The students are happy.
freind, beautifull, wich, untill, recieve, beggining
friend, beautiful, which, until, receive, beginning

blocks.text: 5. Choosing better words (without showing off)

items: good → useful / enjoyable / helpful / impressive
choose the word that says exactly what you mean
bad → disappointing / unhealthy / dangerous / boring
say HOW it was bad
very big → huge / enormous
one strong adjective is better than "very" + a weak one
very happy → delighted / thrilled
for emails, blogs and diaries
a lot of people → crowds of / dozens of / hundreds of
more precise
go → travel / head to / visit
avoid repeating the same verb
nice → peaceful / friendly / delicious / colourful
match the noun: a peaceful place, a delicious meal
think → believe / feel / am convinced
for opinions in Q3 and Q4

blocks.text: Common mistakes on the whole paper

rows: Partial coverage: no top content level
Number the bullets. Tick each one when you finish it
Long social chat at the start of a letter or email
Uses words, adds nothing to the task
Answer bullet 1 in the first or second sentence
Writing an address or date on the letter
Not needed (the task says so) and wastes time
Spelling mistakes lower the 3 language marks
Use words you can spell with 100% confidence
Memorised paragraphs that do not fit the task
Learn useful structures, not whole paragraphs
Answers far below the word range
Thin detail, not enough language to judge
Hit at least the minimum of the range
Less time for Q4. More chances for errors
Keep close to the range and move on
Wrong register ("Hey guys!" to the head teacher)
Decide formal or informal before you write
Running out of time for Q4
Follow the timing plan and watch the clock
Easy spelling and punctuation marks are lost
Keep 2-3 minutes after each question and 5 at the end

blocks.title: كيف تحصل على الدرجة النهائية في الـ Writing
items: قسّم وقتك حسب الدرجات: 10 دقائق للسؤال الأول، و14 للثاني، و20 للثالث، و26 للرابع، و5 دقائق للمراجعة.
في السؤال الأول تُعطى درجات اللغة على الإملاء وعلامات الترقيم فقط، فاكتب جملاً سهلة وصحيحة.
من السؤال الثاني يجب أن تنوّع: جمل مركبة (because – although – which – when) وأزمنة مختلفة وأدوات ربط.
راجع: كل جملة تبدأ بحرف كبير وتنتهي بنقطة، ولا تفصل بين جملتين بفاصلة فقط.

blocks.text: Quick check: test yourself

items.q: How many marks are for Language on the whole Writing paper, and how many for Content?
In Q1, what does the Language mark assess?
items.a: Only spelling and punctuation (3 marks). Vocabulary range is not rewarded in Q1, so write simple, accurate English.

items.q: A student covers only two of the three bullet points in Q2 but writes beautifully. Can they get 6/6 for content?
items.a: No. Missing a compulsory point is partial coverage, so the answer cannot reach the top content level.

items.q: Is there a penalty for writing 95 words in a 70-90 word task?
items.a: No. Word counts are approximate and every word is credited. But keep close to the range: extra words take time and often add mistakes.

items.q: Which question should get the most time, and roughly how long?
items.a: Q4 (23 marks): about 26 minutes including planning and checking.

items.q: Are the two bullet points in Q4 compulsory?
items.a: No. In Q4 they are prompts to help you. In Q2 and Q3 the bullets are compulsory.

items.q: Does a heading on your article or a sign-off on your letter earn a mark?
items.a: No. Layout and text-type features earn no marks by themselves. Marks come from content, clarity, detail, audience awareness and language.
The examiner chooses the level whose description matches the answer best overall, without picking holes in small parts, and then uses the strengths and weaknesses to choose a mark inside that level.
